profile.name: robot
profile.tagline: Mechanical illusion street dance built on abrupt stops, rigid limbs, and motor clicks.
profile.insight: On November 3, 1973, fourteen-year-old Michael Jackson froze mid-song on Soul Train, turning street mime into a global music phenomenon.
profile.profile: The robot, also called the mannequin or dancing machine, is an illusionary street dance style that mimics the stilted mechanics of an automaton. Originating through theatrical pantomime and late-1960s social dancers in American funk clubs, the dance relies on abrupt stops called dimestops to suggest mechanical motors starting and stopping. Although frequently intertwined with popping, the robot stands as its own distinct performance discipline, executed either socially to music or silently as street mime. It achieved worldwide fame during the 1970s following high-profile television performances by The Jackson 5.
profile.profile_long:
The robot, also known as the mannequin or dancing machine, is an illusionary street dance discipline built on the precise simulation of mechanical bodies. Developed at the crossroads of theatrical pantomime and African American social dancing, the style imitates the stilted, segmented movements of automatons, dolls, and machines. During the 1920s, stage mimes had already begun incorporating puppet and automaton routines to comment on the expanding industrial age. By the late 1960s, street performers such as Robert Shields brought mechanical man pantomime to public prominence outside venues like the Hollywood Wax Museum in Los Angeles. Dancers operating in club settings observed these pantomimic techniques and adapted them to the syncopated rhythms of soul and funk.

Key innovators translated solo mime illusions into popular social dance environments. Charles Washington, who adopted the moniker Charles 'Robot' Washington, alongside his partner Robot Ann, transformed the technique into an interactive couple dance at community parties and social clubs. James Higgins, known as Skeeter Rabbit, noted that social robot dancing developed along two lines: pantomimic performers executing machine acts for audiences on the street, and club dancers matching automaton illusions to soul beats as couples. As street dance evolved across California, the robot intertwined closely with popping and locking, pioneered by dancers like Don Campbell. Poppers incorporated the robot's rigid isolations into their broader routines, often adding sharp muscular pops to punctuate the mechanical illusion.

The dance relies on strict physical mechanics. Every isolated gesture begins and ends with an abrupt halt known as a dimestop, or a locking stop, evoking the sensation of small electric motors engaging and disengaging. Throughout a routine, the practitioner maintains an upright, rigid posture, isolating one joint or limb segment at a time. The most accomplished dancers retain the external illusion of metallic stiffness while staying internally relaxed enough to shift cleanly between axes. While the style requires no specific partnering holds, social practitioners historically danced as mirrored pairs or in unison formations. In September 2009, this unison capability was demonstrated on a mass scale when 318 participants organised by Robogals set a Guinness World Record at the University of Melbourne.

Musically, the robot pairs most effectively with precise, heavily articulated beats found in electrofunk, soul, and robo trance. Performers also execute the dance a cappella, vocalising beatbox rhythms, clicks, and simulated servomotor whirs to rhythmically drive their physical isolations. The style entered mainstream popular culture in March 1973 when The Jackson 5 performed 'Dancing Machine'. On November 3, 1973, fourteen-year-old Michael Jackson demonstrated the robot during the song's musical break on the television show Soul Train, later repeating the routine on The Mike Douglas Show, The Sonny and Cher Comedy Hour, and The Carol Burnett Show. The broadcast established the dance worldwide, cementing its vocabulary across television, theatrical film, music videos, and street dance culture.

sections.origins_and_history: Pantomime traditions of imitating mannequins and mechanical figures date back to the 1920s, mirroring the rise of the industrial machine age. In the late 1960s, street mime Robert Shields performed mechanical man illusions at the Hollywood Wax Museum in Los Angeles, inspiring urban dancers to integrate rigid isolations into soul and funk environments. Charles Washington, performing under the name Charles 'Robot' Washington, teamed with partner Robot Ann to adapt mechanical pantomime into a social partner dance at private parties and clubs. The dance gained national and international visibility in 1973 when Michael Jackson, performing with The Jackson 5, showcased the robot on Soul Train, The Mike Douglas Show, and other national television broadcasts.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dancer holds a rigid, upright posture and isolates individual limbs, rotating or shifting joints along strict geometric planes. Each motion begins and ends with a dimestop—a sudden, absolute freeze—or a locking pause that gives the illusion of mechanical gears engaging and halting. Practitioners may add muscular pops on the rhythmic beat while preserving a stiff, automated silhouette. While frequently danced as a solo street illusion or social partner dance, dancers also perform in synchronised unison lines. When performed without musical accompaniment, the discipline operates directly as theatrical mime.
sections.music_and_instruments: The robot is danced to music with distinct, steady rhythms, particularly funk, soul, electrofunk, and robo trance. Performers also dance to songs themed around robotics, such as Styx's 'Mr. Roboto', or perform a cappella, generating their own robotic motor sound effects, clicks, and beatbox percussion. Prominent historical tracks include 'Dancing Machine' by The Jackson 5 and funk tracks by James Brown.
sections.costume_and_setting: Historically performed in everyday street clothes, social party attire, or formal stage costumes worn by musical groups on television broadcasts. Performers also dance in theatrical robot outfits or character costumes, such as in music videos or street theatre outside tourist venues like the Hollywood Wax Museum. The dance occurs in street squares, social dance clubs, television studios, and stage arenas.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally staged as theatrical street mime and later shared as a popular novelty social dance at parties, clubs, and television specials. The movement reflects artistic fascination with automation, robotics, and industrial technology, translating mechanical rigidity into athletic urban expression.
sections.notable_figures: Robert Shields, Charles 'Robot' Washington, Robot Ann, Michael Jackson, Damita Jo Freeman, Don Campbell, James Brown, and James Higgins (Skeeter Rabbit).
sections.regional_variants: Social couple dancing in Californian funk clubs; solo street theatre pantomime in Los Angeles; synchronised ensemble routines developed internationally for stage and world record events.
sections.lineage: Evolved from early 20th-century theatrical mime, puppeting, and mechanical doll pantomime; merged into African American funk and soul social dancing in the late 1960s; later cross-pollinated with popping and locking.

basic_steps: Assume a rigid, upright neutral stance with feet planted and core engaged.
Initiate a single-limb isolation along an angular plane, moving at a constant rate.
Execute a dimestop, abruptly freezing the limb to simulate a motor shutting down.
Optionally add a rhythmic pop on the musical pulse while preserving the rigid silhouette.
Repeat the sequence across the head, neck, arms, or torso sequentially rather than fluidly.
teaching.rhythm: Strict, steady pulse matching funk, electrofunk, or internal a cappella vocal beats.
teaching.formation: Solo performance, social couple dancing, or synchronised unison lines.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners focus on the abrupt stop (dimestop) and keeping the non-moving body parts completely still during isolations.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Heavy, distinct syncopated beat with sharp accents suitable for robotic stops.
music_profile.vocal_style: Soulful lead vocals, spoken automaton lines, or a cappella mouth clicks and beatbox mechanical sounds.
music_profile.musical_form: Verse-chorus funk arrangement with instrumental breaks tailored for solo dance demonstration.
music_profile.sound_description: Distinct, highly regular rhythmic pulses driven by heavy bass lines, crisp snare hits, and electric synthesizer accents. Music often incorporates electrofunk grooves or sparse funk breaks where physical stops align with sudden percussive strikes and simulated machine clicks.

movement_profile.posture: Rigid, upright posture held throughout the performance, with controlled muscle tone to maintain the illusion of mechanical parts.
movement_profile.footwork: Stilted, stepped foot placements that start and halt sharply on rigid angles without fluid weight shifts.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Segmented arm extensions and angular elbow bends that move independently and freeze with abrupt dimestops.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Isolated torso tilts and rotational freezes, avoiding fluid pelvic rolling or natural body waves.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Linear pathways, spot turns, or fixed-station mime presentation in solo, partner, or line setups.
movement_profile.partnering: Social couple dancing performed as mirrored mechanical interactions without traditional partner holds.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Segmented and staccato, contrasting sustained mechanical pacing with instantaneous stops.

signature_moves.name: dimestop
signature_moves.description: A very abrupt stop executed at the start or completion of a movement to simulate a motor starting and stopping.

signature_moves.name: pop on beat
signature_moves.description: A sharp muscular contraction hitting the musical beat while holding a rigid mechanical silhouette.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Primarily danced upright at standing level, without acrobatic jumps.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid fluid, continuous body rolls or casual slouching, which instantly break the illusion of an automaton.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Man Who Froze Time on Soul Train
episode_brief.logline: How street mime pantomime in 1960s California collided with funk rhythm to birth the world's most enduring mechanical dance.
beats: Open outside the Hollywood Wax Museum in the late 1960s with Robert Shields demonstrating mechanical man pantomime to astonished crowds.
Shift to Los Angeles soul clubs where Charles 'Robot' Washington and Robot Ann adapt mechanical mime into an energetic social couple dance.
Recreate the television studio soundstage on November 3, 1973, as Michael Jackson unleashes the robot on Soul Train during 'Dancing Machine'.
Demonstrate the anatomical illusion of the dimestop in a studio mirror, showing how muscles tense and release to simulate an electric servo.
Conclude at the University of Melbourne in 2009 where hundreds of dancers move in mechanical unison to set a Guinness World Record.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master the abrupt start-stop mechanic in isolation.
drills: Extend one forearm outward along a flat plane and halt abruptly on count 1.
Hold the arm motionless for count 2, maintaining rigid tension.
Rotate the wrist 90 degrees on count 3 and dimestop instantly on count 4.

lesson_ladder.goal: Disassociate head turning from torso movement with robotic stillness.
drills: Turn the head 45 degrees to the right in one sharp count, stopping dead on the click.
Follow by turning the torso 45 degrees on the next count while keeping the neck stationary.
Combine head nods and chest shifts in segmented 4-count cycles.

lesson_ladder.goal: Travel across space while integrating pops and mechanical stops.
drills: Step forward with the right heel on count 1, locking the knee sharply.
Follow with the left foot on count 2, finishing with an instant dimestop.
Add a popping pulse through the arms and chest on every even beat while advancing.

visual_motifs: The glowing Soul Train studio stage
Mirrored dancer reflections freezing in exact unison
episode_brief.instructor_persona: A seasoned street dance historian and popper who teaches with surgical geometric precision and historical clarity.
episode_brief.music_cue: An electrofunk groove with crisp percussion, snapping snares, and metallic sound-effect clicks.

connections.name: popping
connections.note: Poppers regularly incorporate the robot into routines by punctuating automaton illusions with muscular pops.

connections.name: locking
connections.note: Robot movements routinely use locking halts to signal the starting and stopping of mechanical motors.

connections.name: puppeting
connections.note: Shares historical lineage with jazz-era pantomime where dancers mimicked wind-up musical box dolls.

seniors.seated_version: Perform isolated 90-degree arm and forearm extensions from a sturdy chair, focusing on sharp wrist turns and hand dimestops without standing.
seniors.standing_version: Stand near a stable bar or chair back; execute head turns and single-arm angular reaches on slow counts without shifting foot placement.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Perform at half-tempo, reducing arm extensions to comfortable chest-level ranges.
seniors.counts: Move on count 1, hold frozen on counts 2 through 4.

children.game_version: Play 'Musical Automaton', where children march like wind-up toys to music and must dimestop into solid statues the moment the beat cuts out.
children.counts: Simple 1-2 robot march counts with a freeze on 3-4.

gaps: Specific BPM tempos are not explicitly provided in the source texts.
Costuming conventions for social club dancers in the late 1960s are only broadly described.

claims.text: The robot mimics the stilted movements of an automaton or mannequin.
claims.quote: suggests the stilted movements of a dancing robot or mannequin.

claims.text: Michael Jackson danced the robot during Dancing Machine with his brothers.
claims.quote: Roboting gained fame in the 1970s after Michael Jackson used the dance when he performed "Dancing Machine" with his brothers.

claims.text: Movements are initiated and concluded with an abrupt dimestop.
claims.quote: Movements of the robot are normally started and finished with a dimestop (a very abrupt stop), to give the impression of motors starting and stopping

claims.text: When performed without musical accompaniment, the illusion is treated as mime.
claims.quote: When done without music, it is considered to be mime, instead of dance.

claims.text: Charles Washington and Robot Ann were the first to dance the style as a social couple dance.
claims.quote: Charles "Robot" Washington and his partner "Robot Ann" were the first to socially couple dance the style to music at parties and clubs.

claims.text: The Jackson 5 debuted the Dancing Machine robot routine on Soul Train on November 3, 1973.
claims.quote: The Jackson 5 first performed "Dancing Machine" on Soul Train on November 3, 1973, where Michael Jackson performed a robot dance during the song's musical break.

claims.text: Robogals organised 318 participants at the University of Melbourne to break the Guinness World Record.
claims.quote: On September 29, 2009, the Guinness World Record for the Largest Robot Dance was broken by Robogals at the University of Melbourne, Australia.

claims.text: Robert Shields inspired Charles Washington to set mechanical mime movements to funk music.
claims.quote: Negli anni '60, un mimo di nome Robert Shields stava facendo decollare la sua carriera a Los Angeles all'Hollywood Wax Museum e ha ispirato un giovane di nome Charles Washington ad adattare quello stile alla musica funk.

claims.text: Skeeter Rabbit noted the dance originated from theatrical machine mimes and people dancing like robots to soul music.
claims.quote: Segundo James Higgins (aka Skeeter Rabbit) pode-se atribuir o surgimento do estilo à duas origens: 1 desde tempos antigos os mímicos fazem vários atos, dentre os quais eles imitam manequins e máquinas. 2 ela evoluiu de pessoas imitando robôs, na batida da música, nas festas e eventos onde se tocava soul music.
